title: STA442
text:
This course is about moving beyond simply knowing how to apply statistical methods and toward thinking carefully about how, when, and why we use them. Throughout the semester, we will work with real-world problems and case studies, with an emphasis on model building, diagnostics, interpretation, and selection. Just as importantly, we will focus on developing the critical thinking and communication skills needed to make sense of statistical results and explain them clearly to others.
Many of you will soon be graduating and moving into careers in industry, research, graduate studies, or other fields. Regardless of where you go next, you may find yourself in situations where others look to you as the statistical expert. My goal is for you to leave this course feeling prepared to take on that responsibility: not because you know every statistical method, but because you know how to think critically about data, question the assumptions behind the models you use, recognize when something has gone wrong, and communicate your conclusions responsibly.
I have high expectations for this course, but I am also committed to creating a welcoming, respectful, and inclusive learning environment where everyone feels comfortable asking questions and contributing to discussions. Please don’t hesitate to ask questions during lectures, office hours, or on Piazza. If you’re struggling with something, reach out early. I am here to support you throughout the semester.
I hope this course helps you develop the confidence to work with data independently and responsibly, and to approach statistical problems with curiosity, care, and a healthy degree of skepticism. I’m looking forward to a great semester with all of you!

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Learning Outcome for This Week
The purpose of this week’s lecture is to ensure that we are on the same page about the basics.

Introduction to statistical models
Designing studies
Introduction to simulations
Procedures of statistical inference

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
section: Big Picture: The Statistical Modelling Workflow
text:
Big Picture: The Statistical Modelling Workflow
Statistical modelling is the process of using data to learn about an unknown population.

1. Population
2. Scientific Question
3. Study Design + Data Collection
4. Statistical Model
5. Estimation
6. Uncertainty Quantification
7. Inference + Scientific Conclusions

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Population
In statistics, a population is the entire group of individuals or objects we are interested in studying.

We collect a sample from the population and use it to make inferences about the population.


Our sample does not contain all observations from the population

Key idea of statistics!
We have limited information (sample) and use it to learn about the unknown population.
If the data are a random sample from a population, we can make reasonable inferences about the population characteristics (e.g. mean)
The key requirement is that the sample should be representative of the population

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Population
It is important to clearly define the population of interest.

it is not enough to say “I collected n observations”
the key question is: Who or what do these observations represent?

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Population
Example 1: Genetic Studies

Many genetic studies have been conducted primarily in people of European ancestry
Models developed using these data often perform poorly in populations with different genetic backgrounds (e.g., people of Asian or African ancestry).


Example 2: Psychology Experiments

Psychology studies often recruit undergraduate students because they are readily accessible.
Do these participants represent all adults?

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Population


In practice, the true characteristics of a population, such as its mean, variance, or distribution, are typically unknown.
Our sample provides limited information about the population, but if it is representative, it can provide a good approximation of the population.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Samples
Random sampling is essential for ensuring that study findings generalize to the population of interest.
Example

In neuroimaging studies, brain MRI scans are often excluded when excessive head motion reduces image quality.
Adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may be more likely to move during scanning and, therefore, more likely to be excluded.
This can introduce selection bias, as the analyzed sample may no longer represent the target population.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Statistical Model
We specify a probability model that represents how we believe the data were generated. This is called the data-generating process (DGP) or data-generating model.


For example, if \[Y_i \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{F}\] then each observation is assumed to be independent and drawn from the same population distribution \(\mathcal{F}\).




One simple model, which makes relatively strong assumptions, is

\[Y_i \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\]

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Examples of Statistical Models
Different research questions require different statistical models!


(linear) \(y_i = \beta_0+ x_i\beta_1 + \epsilon_i\)
(non-linear) \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1sin(x_i) + \epsilon_i\)
(multiple non-linear) \(y_i = f_1(x_{1i}) + f_2(x_{2i}) + ... + f_p(x_{pi}) + \epsilon_i\)
(multiple non-linear with interactions) \(y_i = f_1(x_{1i}) + f_2(x_{2i}) + ... + f_p(x_{pi}) + g_1(f_1(x_{1i})f_2(x_{2i})) +...+ \epsilon_i\)

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Statistical Model

(Binary response)
\[y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}\left( \frac{\exp{(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_i)}}{1 + \exp{(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_i)}}\right)\] Note: this is the default model fit by assuming in glm(..., family = binomial) for binary response data



(Binary data, non linear)

\[y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}\left( \frac{\exp{(\beta_0 + \beta_1\sin(x_i))}}{1 + \exp{(\beta_0 + \beta_1\sin(x_i))}}\right)\]

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Comments on the Statistical Model

“All models are wrong, but some are useful” (George Box)



Standard errors, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests all assume that the statistical model has been correctly specified.

They do not account for errors caused by choosing the wrong model





Statistics is not assumption-free!

We make assumptions that we believe are reasonable approximations to reality.
If these assumptions are substantially violated, the consequences may include:

biased estimates
incorrect standard errors
invalid statistical inference






Does this make statistical methods useless?

No, many statistical procedures are surprisingly robust to modest violations of their assumptions.
We can evaluate through simulations

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Comments on the Statistical Model
Example: Suppose we want to compare the mean outcome before and after treatment using paired observations.

For subject \(i = 1, ..., n\), measured at visits \(j = 1, 2\), suppose we assume
\[ Y_{ij} \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu_j, \sigma^2) \] and test \(H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2\).


What assumption does this model make about repeated measurements from the same subject?



Is that assumption reasonable?
What are the consequences if it is violated?

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Design of Studies

Specify the statistical model

Propose a DGP that is a reasonable approximation of reality
Define the research question and hypothesis
Plan the study design (e.g., sampling strategy and sample size)




Collect the data

Obtain a (ideally random) sample from the population of interest





Estimate the quantities of interest

Estimate the unknown parameters (e.g., using maximum likelihood estimation)
Quantify the uncertainty in these estimates (e.g., standard errors or confidence intervals)





Draw statistical conclusions

Construct appropriate test statistics or confidence intervals
Make conclusions about the population based on observed data

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Design of Studies
In practice…


The assumed model does not have to be the true DGP, it only needs to be a useful approximation
If the sample size is small or estimation is unstable, regularization (penalization) may improve estimation
If analytic uncertainty quantification is difficult, resampling methods (e.g., the bootstrap) can often be used

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Design of Studies
Some cautionary notes


Ideally, the statistical model and hypotheses are specified before examining the data.

This is informed by background knowledge, scientific theory, and previous research.
If we repeatedly explore the data until we find an interesting pattern, we may discover relationships that are due to chance rather than true effects.





A planned analysis may still be inappropriate after data collection.

Model assumptions should be checked after observing the data.
If assumptions are violated, we may need to modify the analysis
These decisions should be transparently reported.





This does not mean we cannot explore data.

Exploratory analyses can identify new patterns, generate hypotheses, and suggest future research directions.
Ideally, these findings should be validated using an independent dataset.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Misusing Statistics
Some common practices that can invalidate statistical inference include:


P-hacking: Trying multiple analyses and only reporting one that produces a statistically significant result
HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known): presenting hypotheses generated from the data as though they were specified before the analysis
Repeated Significance Testing: repeated analyzing the data as participants are recruited and stopping once a significant result is obtained
Post-hoc Participant Exclusion: Modifying inclusion or exclusion criteria after examining the data
Using Inappropriate Statistical Methods: applying statistical tests that do not match the study design, outcome type, or model assumptions
Overfitting: including predictors without scientific justification or appropriate model selection.



Key Point: Statistical inference depends on the entire analysis process. Even a perfectly computed p-value can be misleading if the study design or analysis is flawed.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Misusing Statistics
“If you torture the data long enough, it will confess to anything” (Ronald Coase)


In principle, the data should be analyzed only once to make confirmatory results. Any other results would be exploratory.
A good understanding of the scientific domain is essential for designing appropriate studies, selecting sample sizes, specifying hypotheses, and choosing suitable statistical analyses.
A solid understanding of statistics helps you choose models that provide valid and informative inference.



The goal is not to obtain a small p-value. The goal is to produce evidence that is scientifically credible and statistically valid.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Case Study: Clinical Trials
Developing a new drug requires substantial time and financial investment.
Phase 3 clinical trials provide the evidence needed for regulatory approval. Because these trials are costly and time-consuming, careful statistical planning is essential.

Poor decisions about:

study design,
sample size,
endpoints,
or statistical analysis

can lead to inconclusive or failed trials, resulting in significant financial losses (i.e., sunk costs) and organizational consequences.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Case Study: Clinical Trials
Potential (direct) consequences of sunk cost?


In 2019, Roche announced plans to cut 500 jobs in Switzerland following the failure of a key clinical trial for its Alzheimer’s drug.
In 2016, The failure of Eli Lilly’s Alzheimer’s drug, solanezumab, in a Phase 3 trial led to significant restructuring and layoffs.
Many others!

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Case Study: Clinical Trials
A Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) promotes transparency, reproducibility, and adherence to regulatory requirements.
The SAP is developed before observing trial outcomes to prevent decisions from being influenced by the results.

Key considerations include:



Study design: sample size, randomization, trial structure, and stopping rules.
Outcomes: primary endpoint selection and hypotheses to be tested.
Analysis methods: statistical models, covariate selection, and software.
Data handling: missing data methods and subgroup analyses.
Multiple comparisons: strategies to control false positive findings.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Main Takeaway

Statistical inference begins before data collection.

A clear research question, appropriate study design, and reasonable statistical model are essential.




Models are approximations of reality.

We do not expect a model to be perfectly true, but it should provide a useful representation of the data-generating process.





The analysis process matters.

Statistical conclusions depend on how data are collected, analyzed, and interpreted—not just on the final statistical test.





Exploration and confirmation are both valuable, but they serve different purposes.

Exploratory analyses generate hypotheses; confirmatory analyses provide evidence for hypotheses.





The goal of statistics is not to find significant results.

The goal is to produce reliable, reproducible, and scientifically meaningful evidence.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Motivating Example

We know from geometry that the area of a unit circle is \(\pi\).
However, determining the value of \(\pi\) has a long history, requiring increasingly sophisticated mathematical methods.
Modern approaches use calculus to derive and compute this quantity.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Motivating Example
How can we estimate the area of a circle using simulation?


Generate random points within the square, \([-1,1] \times [-1,1]\).




The probability that a point falls inside the circle is equal to the ratio of the two areas, \(A/4\).




Repeat this process many times and estimate the probability by the proportion of points that fall inside the circle.



If \(M\) out of 50,000 points fall inside the circle:
\[
\frac{A}{4} \approx \frac{M}{50000}
\]
Therefore:
\[
A \approx 4 \times \frac{M}{50000}
\]

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Motivating Example

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Motivating Example
Using 50,000 simulated points:
\[\hat{\pi}=3.14432\]

The estimate is not exactly \(\pi\), but it is close!
Because the estimate is based on random sampling, it will vary from simulation to simulation.
Increasing the number of simulated points reduces this variability and gives a more precise estimate.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Why simulate?

We can specify a population to generate random samples

We then can evaluate statistical properties such as bias of an estimate, errors associated with hypothesis testing, coverage probabilities, etc.


Later, we will use simulations to see what happens if

the model is misspecified

sample size isn’t sufficient
statistical misbehaviour is made (e.g. p-hacking)
etc.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations

Using simulations, we can generate a population that is bell-shaped, with a fixed mean (e.g., 5) and variance (e.g., 1).

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
A simple example: generating random data in R

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Designing Simulation Studies
A simulation study should be carefully designed to answer a specific statistical question.

A useful framework is ADEMP (Morris et al., 2019):


A — Aim: What statistical question are we trying to answer?
D — Data-generating mechanism: How will we generate the simulated data?
E — Estimands: What quantities are we interested in evaluating?
M — Methods: What statistical procedures are being evaluated or compared?
P — Performance measures: How will we assess the methods?





 Morris, T. P., White, I. R., & Crowther, M. J. (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. Statistics in Medicine, 38(11), 2074–2102.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Example: Evaluating ‘Unbiasedness’ Empirically
Assume the following model:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \epsilon_i \quad \text{where} \quad \epsilon_i \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]
Using the ADEMP framework…


A — Aim: Is the coefficient \(\beta_1\) of a linear regression model unbiased?
D — Data-generating mechanism: We fix \(\beta_0, \beta_1\), and generate a dataset \((x_i, y_i), i=1, ..., n\) where each \(X_i \sim Uniform(0,5)\). We also generate \(\epsilon_i \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\).
E — Estimands: We estimate \(\beta_1\)
M — Methods: Fitting a linear regression model.
P — Performance measures: Bias (i.e. \(E[\hat{\beta}_1] - \beta_1\)))

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Example: Evaluating ‘Unbiasedness’ Empirically

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations
Example: Evaluating ‘Unbiasedness’ Empirically
Let’s repeat this process 1,000 times and calculate the average of all estimated \(\beta_1\) values to estimate the bias.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Hypothesis Testing
In statistics, a hypothesis is a statement of one or more parameters

e.g., \(H_0: E(X_i) = 100\) and \(H_A: E(X_i) \neq 100\)


The method of hypothesis testing uses data from a sample to judge whether a statement about a population may be true or not.

A simple way you learned is to somehow get a p-value, and compare it to a significance level, \(\alpha\)
If the p-value is less than \(\alpha\), we reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Errors in Hypothesis Testing
Since we are making conclusions about the population with limited information, our decision is always prone to some errors.

Type 1 Error: False positive; rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually true

P(Type 1 Error) = \(\alpha\)



Type 2 Error: False negative; failing to reject the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually false

P(Type 2 Error) = \(\beta\)



Power: the probability that a test will correctly reject a null hypothesis that is false

Related to Type 2 Error
Power = 1 - P(Type 2 Error) = \(1 - \beta\)



Ideally, you want to reduce these two errors, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) as much as possible.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Errors in Hypothesis Testing
Type I Error
A Type I error occurs when we reject \(H_0\), even though \(H_0\) is true.
\[
P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true}) = \alpha
\]

The value \(\alpha\) is called the significance level of the test.


We choose \(\alpha\) in advance, which allows us to control the Type I error rate.
A common choice is
\[
\alpha = 0.05.
\]

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Errors in Hypothesis Testing
Power
The power of a hypothesis test is the probability of correctly rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false.
\[
P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is false}) = 1 - \beta
\]

A test with high power is more likely to detect a real effect when one exists.


Power depends on:

the sample size
the effect size
the significance level, \(\alpha\)

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Simulations: Statistical Inference
Case 1: Behaviours of p-values when \(H_0\) is true, \(n=50\)
We want to test the following hypothesis: \[H_0: \mu = 5 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_A: \mu \neq 5\] We draw 50 samples from a population that has a mean of 5, i.e., we are setting up a scenario where the null hypothesis is true.
Then, using the simulated data, we test the hypothesis.

Power
Remember, when talking about power we are assuming the null hypothesis is false (i.e., the alternative is true)

Above, we see clearly that \(\alpha\), the effect size and sample size have an effect on power.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Empirical Understanding of Statistics
Simulation lets us ask: What actually happens?
We can use simulation to investigate the behaviour of statistical methods when:


assumptions are violated
e.g., non-normal or skewed errors




sample sizes are small
e.g., does the Type I error rate remain at \(\alpha\)?




models are misspecified
e.g., ignoring within-subject correlation




we want to evaluate statistical properties
e.g., bias, power, or confidence interval coverage

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Summary

Throughout the course, we will return to the same questions:

What assumptions does the model make?
How do we estimate uncertainty?
How well does the model represent the data-generating process?

We will use simulations to investigate the properties of statistical methods and evaluate how well they perform under different scenarios.

title: STA442
text:
This course is about moving beyond simply knowing how to apply statistical methods and toward thinking carefully about how, when, and why we use them. Throughout the semester, we will work with real-world problems and case studies, with an emphasis on model building, diagnostics, interpretation, and selection. Just as importantly, we will focus on developing the critical thinking and communication skills needed to make sense of statistical results and explain them clearly to others.
Many of you will soon be graduating and moving into careers in industry, research, graduate studies, or other fields. Regardless of where you go next, you may find yourself in situations where others look to you as the statistical expert. My goal is for you to leave this course feeling prepared to take on that responsibility: not because you know every statistical method, but because you know how to think critically about data, question the assumptions behind the models you use, recognize when something has gone wrong, and communicate your conclusions responsibly.
I have high expectations for this course, but I am also committed to creating a welcoming, respectful, and inclusive learning environment where everyone feels comfortable asking questions and contributing to discussions. Please don’t hesitate to ask questions during lectures, office hours, or on Piazza. If you’re struggling with something, reach out early. I am here to support you throughout the semester.
I hope this course helps you develop the confidence to work with data independently and responsibly, and to approach statistical problems with curiosity, care, and a healthy degree of skepticism. I’m looking forward to a great semester with all of you!

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Population

We are often interested in numerical summaries that describe a population.

These numerical summaries are called parameters

e.g. mean height of all UofT students
Although the parameter is unknown, it is a fixed (constant) value.

The corresponding summaries computed from a sample are called statistics.




Since our conclusions are based on a sample rather than the entire population, every statistical conclusion involves some uncertainty.

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Warm-Up Questions
For paired data, an independent two-sample (t)-test is just as appropriate as a paired (t)-test.
True or false?


If a regression model gives (p > 0.05), it is reasonable to remove a variable and refit the model until (p < 0.05).
True or false?



If 846 out of 20,000 hypothesis tests have (p < 0.05), we can conclude that those 846 effects are real.
True or false?

title: Statistical Modelling and Inference
text:
Warm-Up Questions
What do you think?

Suppose I apply to 20 PhD programs, and each program has an acceptance rate of 20/%.
If the decisions were independent, then
\[
P(\text{at least one acceptance})
=
1-(1-0.20)^{20}
\approx 0.988.
\]
So, do I really have a 98.8% chance of getting into at least one program?

What assumption is being made here? Is it reasonable?

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Today’s Lecture
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Explain the logic of a permutation test and construct a permutation-based null distribution.
Describe why conducting many hypothesis tests increases the risk of false-positive findings.
Compare family-wise error rate (FWER) and false discovery rate (FDR), and identify when each is appropriate.
Apply Bonferroni and FDR adjustments to account for multiple comparisons.
Recognize how inappropriate selection and testing practices can inflate error rates and reported effect sizes.

Motivating Example
Researchers have developed a new drug that inhibits a mouse’s ability to run through a maze. Using three mice receiving the drug and three controls receiving a placebo, they measured the time required to complete the maze.

The two-sample \(t\)-test gives a \(p\)-value of approximately \(0.122\).

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Why Consider a Permutation Test?
With such a small sample, the parametric \(p\)-value may be unreliable.
Can we test the hypothesis without relying as heavily on parametric assumptions?


A permutation test is a non-parametric method that tests a null hypothesis by “rearranging” the observed data.

Key Idea: If \(H_0\) is true (there is no difference between the population means) then swapping the group labels should not make a systematic difference.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Permutation Test: Procedure


State the null hypothesis.
Calculate the test statistic from the observed data.
Shuffle (permute) the data: Under the null hypothesis, the grouping or labeling of the data is arbitrary. Therefore, repeatedly shuffle or permute the data to create new datasets where the null hypothesis holds true.
Recalculate the test statistic for each permutation: After each shuffle, calculate the test statistic on the permuted data.
Use the permuted statistics to construct the null distribution.
Compute the \(p\)-value as the proportion of permuted statistics at least as extreme as the observed statistic.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Connection to Parametric Tests

Parametric and permutation tests differ mainly in how they obtain the null distribution (the distribution of the test statistic under \(H_0\)).

Parametric: obtained by deriving the distributional properties (assumptions)
Permutation: obtained by a data-driven manner (e.g. without assuming CLT or distributional form of a population)

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Correlation or Simple Linear Regression
Suppose we are testing
\[
H_0:\rho_{XY}=0
\]
for the simple linear regression \(Y\sim X\).
Under \(H_0\), we can randomly shuffle the order of \(X\) to break its relationship with \(Y\) while preserving the observed values of both variables.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Multiple Regression
Consider
\[
y_i=\beta_0+x_i\beta_1+z_i\beta_2+w_i\beta_3+\epsilon_i,
\qquad
H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0.
\]
Here, \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) describe the effects of \(x_i\) and \(z_i\) on \(E(Y_i)\) while controlling for \(w_i\).

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
section: Multiple Regression: What Should We Shuffle?
text:
Multiple Regression: What Should We Shuffle?

We cannot shuffle \(w_i\): this does not break the relationship between \((x_i,z_i)\) and \(y_i\).
We should not shuffle \(y_i\): this also breaks the relationship between \(y_i\) and \(w_i\).
We should not shuffle \(x_i\) and \(z_i\) separately: their dependence should be preserved.
We can shuffle the pairs \((x_i,z_i)\) together. This preserves their mutual dependence and leaves the relationship between \(y_i\) and \(w_i\) intact.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Permutation Tests: Summary

Few distributional assumptions: Unlike a parametric test, a permutation test does not assume a particular population distribution.
Versatile: It can be used with many statistics, including differences in means, medians, variances, and correlations.
Computationally intensive: Many permutations may be needed, especially for large datasets.

We need to take care when permutating as to not break relationships that are allowed under the null hypothesis

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
The Jelly Bean Experiment


Do jelly beans cause acne?

We could conduct a randomized experiment and compare the mean number of acne lesions between treatment and control groups.
Suspecting that the relationship may depend on jelly bean colour, we test each colour separately.

15 colours \(\Rightarrow\) 15 two-sample \(t\)-tests.
For each colour, reject \(H_0\) when \(p<0.05\).






This is a pedagogical example, not an actual study.



Question: What problem might arise?

text:
The Dead Salmon Experiment
In this experiment:

The brain of a dead Atlantic salmon was scanned in an MRI machine.
The salmon was presented with an open-ended mentalizing task.
The imaging data were analyzed using a standard fMRI pipeline.
Each voxel was modeled separately using a GLM, producing a \(p\)-value at every location.


Bennett, C. M., Miller, M. B., & Wolford, G. L. (2009). Neural correlates of interspecies perspective taking in the post-mortem Atlantic Salmon: An argument for multiple comparisons correction. Neuroimage, 47(Suppl 1), S125.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
section: How Often Do We Get a False Positive?
text:
How Often Do We Get a False Positive?








When 50 null hypotheses are tested separately at \(\alpha=0.05\), there is approximately a 92% chance of observing at least one false positive.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Accounting for Multiple Comparisons
Two common ways to address multiple comparisons are:

Family-wise error rate (FWER)
False discovery rate (FDR)

The choice between FWER and FDR should depend on the research context and the goal of the analysis.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER)

The Type I error rate describes a single hypothesis test.
The family-wise error rate (FWER) is the probability of making at least one false positive across a family of tests.
FWER guards against any false positive: “none versus at least one.”

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
What Determines the FWER?

Number of tests: More tests require a more stringent threshold.
Desired FWER: Often set to 5%.



If 20 independent null hypotheses are each tested at \(\alpha=0.05\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(\text{at least one false positive})
&= 1 - P(\text{no false positives}) \\
&= 1 - (1 - 0.05)^{20} \\
&= 1 - (0.95)^{20} \\
&\approx 1 - 0.3585 \\
&\approx 0.6415.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Bonferroni Correction
To control the FWER at level \(\alpha\) across \(m\) tests, use the per-test threshold
\[
\alpha^*=\frac{\alpha}{m}.
\]
Then, by the union bound,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{FWER}
&=P_{H_0}\!\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}
\left\{p_j\leq\frac{\alpha}{m}\right\}\right)\\
&\leq\sum_{j=1}^{m}P_{H_0}\!\left(p_j\leq\frac{\alpha}{m}\right)\\
&=m\left(\frac{\alpha}{m}\right)=\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Bonferroni Correction: Properties

Simple and guaranteed to control FWER: \(\operatorname{FWER}\leq\alpha\).
Can be conservative because the bound may be strict.
In the dead salmon study, \(p<0.001\) would control FWER at 5% only if there were 50 tests:

\[
0.001=\frac{0.05}{50}.
\]
With many more voxels, that threshold is too loose.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Permutation-Based FWER Control








Permutation-based FWER control accounts for dependence among the tests and does not require independent \(p\)-values.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Permutation-Based FWER Control

For each permutation \(b=1,\ldots,B\):

Shuffle the subject labels under \(H_0\).
Calculate all \(m\) test statistics \(t_1^{(b)},\ldots,t_m^{(b)}\).
Store only the maximum:

\[
T^{(b)}=\max\left\{t_1^{(b)},\ldots,t_m^{(b)}\right\}.
\]
The collection \(T^{(1)},\ldots,T^{(B)}\) forms a null distribution for the maximum statistic.

text: Permutation-Based FWER Control in R

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Permutation-Based FWER Control








Permutation-based FWER control accounts for dependence among the tests and does not require independent \(p\)-values.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
False Discovery Rate (FDR)
Controlling FWER can be conservative, and there is a relevant concept of false positive rates in multiple comparisons: False Discovery Rate (FDR).

When \(m\) hypotheses are tested, each test belongs to one of four categories \((V, U, S, W )\):

Ideally, we want to minimize the number of false positive \((V)\)

False Discovery Rate (FDR)

FDR controls the expected proportion of false positives among the hypotheses you rejected \((V/R)\).


If FDR is controlled at 5%, approximately 5% of the statistically significant findings are expected to be false positives in the long run.

FDR is more lenient than FWER: it tolerates some false positives in exchange for greater ability to identify real effects.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
FDR Adjustment in R

Choose the desired FDR level, such as 5%.
Obtain the raw \(p\)-values.
Use p.adjust() to calculate FDR-adjusted \(p\)-values.
Declare adjusted \(p\)-values below 0.05 significant.









In this example, hypotheses 1 and 4 are rejected.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
section: When Should We Choose FWER or FDR?
text:
When Should We Choose FWER or FDR?
Make this choice before analyzing the data to avoid p-hacking.


General recommendations:

Use FWER when you care about the specific hypotheses being tested, i.e. you want to minimize the risk of any false positives for individual comparisons.
Choose FDR when you care more about the number of significant findings (for further investigations) rather than the specific hypotheses.




Do not choose FDR simply because it produces more significant findings.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
An Apparently Reasonable Analysis
Suppose an fMRI dataset contains 100,000 voxels.

Remove voxels with “uninteresting” correlations, such as \(|r|<0.5\), leaving 500 voxels.
Apply Bonferroni correction only to those 500 voxels and analyze the voxels satisfying \(p<\frac{0.05}{500}.\)

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
section: What’s Wrong with the Previous Analysis?
text:
What’s Wrong with the Previous Analysis?

Double dipping: The same data were used first to select the 500 strongest correlations and then to test them.
The procedure resembles a multiple-comparison correction, but it does not properly control FWER.



Valid alternatives:

Pre-specify the 500 voxels before examining the data, then test them using \(p<0.05/500\).
Apply Bonferroni correction to all 100,000 voxels using \(p<0.05/100000\).

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
“Voodoo” Correlations
Some fMRI studies of emotion, personality, and social cognition reported extremely high (sometimes greater than 0.8) correlations between brain activation and personality measures.


Neuroimaging measurements are noisy and often have low reliability.
Behavioural measurements, such as reaction time and accuracy, are also noisy.
How can two noisy measurements correlate above 0.8, sometimes with fewer than 25 subjects?



Vul, E., Harris, C., Winkielman, P., & Pashler, H. (2009). Puzzlingly high correlations in fMRI studies of emotion, personality, and social cognition. Perspectives on psychological science, 4(3), 274-290.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
section: Simulation: A Correlation of 0.8 by Chance
text:
Simulation: A Correlation of 0.8 by Chance

Simulate 40,000 features for each of 20 subjects.
Simulate an unrelated behavioural measure for the same subjects.
Calculate the correlation between the behaviour and each feature.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Distribution of the 40,000 Correlations








Even though every population correlation is zero, the largest sample correlation can be close to 0.8.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
The Most Highly Correlated Feature








The fitted red line is a severely inflated sample effect created by selecting the largest of 40,000 correlations. The true population relationship is flat.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Lessons from the Simulation

Passing a stringent threshold is difficult, for example, Bonferroni gives \(\frac{0.05}{40000}=1.25\times10^{-6}.\)
Nevertheless, when FWER is controlled at 5%, a false positive can still occur with probability up to 5%.
If a feature passes the threshold by chance, its reported sample effect size may appear very large even though the population effect is zero.
Effect sizes from features selected after many comparisons can be severely inflated.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
Lecture Summary

Permutation tests build a null distribution by rearranging the observed data under \(H_0\).
When testing many hypotheses, the chance of at least one false positive can be much larger than the per-test Type I error rate.
FWER controls the probability of any false positive; FDR controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among rejected hypotheses.
Bonferroni is simple but can be conservative; permutation methods can account for dependence among tests.
Selection and testing with the same data can inflate error rates and effect-size estimates.

A genome-wide association study fits a model relating a trait (e.g. cholesterol level) to each genetic variant.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
FWER Method 1: Bonferroni Correction

Bonferronni correction is very simple and guaranteed to control FWER: (\(\operatorname{FWER}\leq\alpha\)).
Can be conservative because the bound may be strict.
In the dead salmon study, \(p<0.001\) would control FWER at 5% only if there were 50 tests:

\[
0.001=\frac{0.05}{50}.
\]
With many more voxels, that threshold is too loose.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
FWER Method 2: Permutation
Controlling FWER is equivalent to setting a threshold for \(p_{\min}=\min\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\}\) or, for one-sided tests, \(T_{\max}=\max\{t_1,\ldots,t_m\}.\)
At least one rejected hypothesis is equivalent to the minimum \(p\)-value crossing its threshold, or the maximum test statistic crossing its threshold.
 

Permuation testing allows us to set a threshold for the maximum test statistic, providing a method to control FWER.
Permutation-based control of FWER is exact, and does not depend on independence assumptions of p values.

title: Topics in Statistical Inference
text:
FWER Method 2: Permutation
Suppose we are testing \(m\) hypotheses simultaneously.

Permutation Procedure

Calculate the observed test statistics: \[
T_1,\ldots,T_m.
\]
Permute the data under \(H_0\) and recompute all \(m\) test statistics.
For permutation \(b\), keep only the most extreme statistic: \[
T_{\max}^{(b)}=\max_j |T_j^{(b)}|.
\]
Repeat for \(b=1,\ldots,B\) to form the null distribution of \(T_{\max}\).
For \(\alpha=0.05\), use the 95th percentile as the cutoff \(c\).
Reject \(H_{0j}\) if \[
|T_j|>c.
\]
